# Review: Zatsiorsky & Kraemer, Science and Practice of Strength Training 2e, Chapters 1-2 (round 1, Opus)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent, falsification brief). Date: 2026-09-27.
Scope: 15 entries plus `_book.md` in `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/`.

## Method and coverage

- Every check below was made against the **page image** of the 2e scan (Read tool, `pages`), never the OCR text. Pages opened: PDF 12-24 (printed 3-15) and PDF 27-55 (printed 18-46). PDF 25-26 (printed 16-17, chapter 2 opener) were not opened; no entry cites them.
- The two-factor equation was re-rendered at 400 and 900 dpi (PyMuPDF crop of PDF p. 22) to read the exponents.
- Offset printed = PDF - 9 confirmed on every page opened.
- 1st-edition check: the 1e copy (Coach Lowe PDF) was probed page by page for text length. **1e PDF pp. 8-31 have zero characters of text layer** (pp. 1, 5 also empty). Key hits elsewhere: "recall the two-factor theory of training in chapter 1" (1e PDF p. 48); "Because of the existence of the explosive strength deficit (see chapter 2...)" (1e PDF p. 54); "The rate of force development (especially the S-gradient) does not correlate with the maximal force" and "The force in exercises with reversible muscle action does not change after heavy resistance training" (1e PDF p. 42); the Zatsiorsky & Raitsin numbers "410 ± 170 N ... 11.5 ± 5.4 kg ... 560 ± 230 N ... 7.5 ± 4.7 kg" (1e PDF p. 7).
- Baseline labels were checked against `docs/method-baseline.md` line by line.
- Dedup: grepped the vault library and the staging library; read the overlapping entries named below.

Note for the fixer: the coordinator's task brief for this review also called the printed p. 27 table "elite time-to-peak-force figures". That label is wrong (see ESD row). Do not "correct" the entry back to it.

## Entry verdicts

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `principle--two-factor-fitness-fatigue-theory-and-training-effects-taxonomy.md` | FIX | (1) **Equation misread.** Entry: "Preparedness = P₀ + P₁e^(−t/k₁) − P₂e^(−t/k₂)", "recovered here from the page image", and "k₁ and k₂ are time constants". Page image (PDF 22 / p. 13, 900 dpi crop): the exponents are **−k₁t** and **−k₂t**, and the book calls k₁, k₂ "time constraints" (sic). The t/k form changes the meaning of k (time constant vs rate constant). (2) **Voice mislabel.** "**Eric's baseline:** Evans's course independently flags the fitness-fatigue model as 'just a concept'". Evans is a library source, not Eric's baseline. (3) **Invented, unlabelled Example.** "a heavy multi-week block can suppress tested performance during the block ... while the delayed effect only shows once fatigue clears". The book gives no such example on pp. 12-15, and it nearly duplicates the vault's Bompa `framework--three-training-effects` Example ("An athlete's vertical jump dips through a heavy three-week block ... then rebounds"). (4) **Baseline mapping stretch.** Entry: "the department's stated in-season rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'". Baseline tags this **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)**, a course-team position. Book (PDF 23 / p. 14): Coach B's idea is "to decrease the training load during each session rather than the number of workouts", with volume vs intensity unspecified, and the contrast is about **tapering/peaking before an important competition**, not in-season maintenance. (5) **Dedup.** No link to the staging Supertraining `framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy`, whose "acute", "particular" and "cumulative" are defined differently from this book's "acute" (during exercise), "partial" (single training means) and "cumulative" (continued sessions or seasons). Checked clean: "more sophisticated than the supercompensation theory" (PDF 21 / p. 12); fitness "does not vary substantially over several minutes, hours, or even days"; "For most crude estimations ... differ by a factor of three ... 24 h ... 72 h" (PDF 22 / p. 13); Coach A two or three sessions in the final week with a relatively large load, Coach B warm-up-type sessions (PDF 23 / p. 14); six effects and their definitions (PDF 23 / p. 14; summary PDF 24 / p. 15). | (1) Replace the equation with `Preparedness = P₀ + P₁e^(−k₁t) − P₂e^(−k₂t)` and the definition with "k₁ and k₂ are what the book calls 'time constraints' (printed p. 13, sic; read as rate constants in this exponent form)". Delete "recovered here from the page image because the OCR text drops..." or keep it only after the corrected form. (2) Change "**Eric's baseline:** Evans's course independently flags" to "A separate library source, Evans's course, flags". (3) Replace the Example with the authors' own Coach A / Coach B taper contrast (move it from When to apply), or prefix "Inference:" and make it differ from Bompa's example. (4) Write "**Eric's baseline** (Inferred, course-team material):" and add to the Inference: "the book's contrast concerns the final days before a main competition, and Coach B cuts 'training load' per session without saying whether volume or intensity; the Baylor rule is an in-season maintenance rule, so the match is partial." (5) Add Related link to `supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy` with one line on the definitional differences (acute vs immediate; partial vs particular; cumulative means continued sessions here, a complex of multi-directional means there). |
| `claim--one-factor-supercompensation-theory-contested-by-the-authors.md` | FIX | (1) **Wrong locator.** "(PDF pp. 20-21, 29-30, printed pp. 11-12, 20-21.)" The one-factor section is printed pp. 10-12 (PDF 19-21); printed 20-21 is chapter 2 and holds nothing about supercompensation. (2) **Overstated wording.** Entry: "Muscle glycogen supercompensation specifically has been demonstrated". Book (PDF 21 / p. 12): "For some metabolites, like muscle glycogen, after-exercise **depletion** has been definitely demonstrated. It is possible to **induce** glycogen supercompensation by combining a proper training routine with carbohydrate loading." (3) Entry: "restoration times for different substances vary by unknown amounts". Book: "requires unequal amounts of time". "Unknown" is not in the text. Checked clean and the `contested` rating is properly grounded in the authors' own words: "The very existence of the supercompensation phase for a majority of metabolic substances has never been experimentally proven" and "In general, the theory of supercompensation is too simple to be correct. Over the last few years it has lost much of its popularity" (both PDF 21 / p. 12); ATP "do not change substantially even after very hard exercise"; "It is absolutely unclear which criteria (substances)..." (PDF 21 / p. 12); overloading microcycle "The common belief is that such a training routine produces a final supercompensation that is greater than normal" (PDF 21 / p. 12; fig 1.6); figs 1.4-1.5 (PDF 19-20 / pp. 10-11). Bompa entry wording ("Contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor...") confirmed in the vault file. | (1) Locator to "(PDF pp. 19-21, printed pp. 10-12.)". (2) "For muscle glycogen, after-exercise depletion has been definitely demonstrated, and glycogen supercompensation can be induced by combining training with carbohydrate loading (printed p. 12)". (3) "restoration of different substances requires unequal amounts of time (printed p. 12)". |
| `framework--four-features-of-the-adaptation-process.md` | FIX | (1) **Invented baseline position.** "**Eric's baseline:** individualization matches Baylor's own department framing that stressors are additive and load must be adjusted per athlete (`method-baseline.md`, 'Strength and power'...)". Nothing about additive stressors or per-athlete load adjustment appears in `method-baseline.md` (grep for "additive" and "individual": no such position). This puts words in Eric's mouth. (2) **False scope claim.** "stated here only as a checklist item, not developed further in this chapter". The book has a full Individualization section (PDF 19 / p. 10): imitating famous athletes' routines has "proven unsuccessful"; understand general ideas, not the entire protocol; "Only average athletes ... prepare with average methods. Champions are not average; they are exceptional." (3) **Dedup miss.** The vault's Evans `framework--three-types-of-overload-stimulating-retaining-detraining` quotes an uncited slide whose wording matches this book's p. 5 bullets almost verbatim ("above the neutral level", "in the neutral zone", "decrease in performance results, in the functional capabilities of the athlete, or both"). Not linked. Checked clean: four-item list (PDF 13 / p. 4); overload two ways, detraining if too low (PDF 13 / p. 4); three load classes (PDF 14 / p. 5; fig 1.1 PDF 13); ~10x, 5,000 tons/yr, 1/10th-1/12th, 8,000-12,000 km vs about 1,000 km (PDF 14 / p. 5); triplets 57.5 kg, 50 kg x5, 60 kg (PDF 14 / p. 5); summary quote "Training programs must be adjusted individually to each athlete. Remember that all people are different." (PDF 24 / p. 15). | (1) Delete the "Eric's baseline:" sentence. If a link is wanted, write "Inference: the baseline has no stated individualization rule; the nearest items are the per-sport battery (Baylor Sport Assessment Table) and body-size-based HR zones (`method-baseline.md`, Testing; Conditioning)", labelled Inference. (2) Replace with a summary of the p. 10 section and add PDF 19 / p. 10 to the locator ("PDF pp. 13-14, 19, 24; printed pp. 4-5, 10, 15"). (3) Add Related `elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--three-types-of-overload-stimulating-retaining-detraining`, and a reciprocal-link suggestion: this book's p. 5 is the likely primary source for Evans's uncited slide. |
| `framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation.md` | FIX | (1) **Self-contradicting voice label.** Why it works opens "Inference: normalizing by each exercise's own population standard deviation..." then ends "The authors state this reasoning directly (printed p. 9) rather than leaving it as this entry's inference." The reasoning is the authors' and it is on printed p. 8 (PDF 17): "As performances in different exercises have different modalities (force, time, distance) and are not directly comparable, a dimensionless unit should be employed". (2) **Missing author caveat that belongs in When NOT to apply** (PDF 18 / p. 9): "Specificity of adaptation increases with the level of sport mastership ... The transfer of training gain is lower in good athletes; for beginners, almost all exercises are useful", and "the training effects were more specific for the group that performed exercise at the 130° knee-joint angle". (3) **Dedup miss.** Vault Supertraining `claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer` cites the same Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) study; not linked. (4) Baseline ODSF cited without the baseline's own tag "Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own ... origin: Hawkin Dynamics". Checked clean: every table value (1310 ± 340, 1720 ± 270, 410 ± 170, 410/340 = 1.2; 95.5 ± 23, 107 ± 21, 11.5 ± 5.4, 11.5/23 = 0.5, 0.42; 2710 ± 618, 3270 ± 642, 560 ± 230, 0.91; 102 ± 28, 110 ± 23, 7.5 ± 4.7, 0.27, 0.30), the "Note the results" table and the concluding quote (PDF 18 / p. 9); result gain and effect-size definitions and the transfer ratio (PDF 17-18 / pp. 8-9); citation Theory and Practice of Physical Culture 6: 7-14 (PDF 17 / p. 8); squat/jump/sprint/swim example (PDF 15 / p. 6). Same data present in the 1e (1e PDF p. 7). | (1) Drop "Inference:" and write "The authors give the reason: performances in different exercises have different modalities and are not directly comparable, so a dimensionless unit is needed (printed p. 8)." (2) Add both p. 9 statements to When NOT to apply with the locator. (3) Add Related link to `supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer` (reciprocal: that entry's secondhand citation has its primary data here). (4) Tag the ODSF mention "(adopted practice, Hawkin Dynamics framework, not Eric's own)". |
| `principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law.md` | FIX | (1) Entry: "using an efficient drill (overhead throwing of a 3-kg shot by a javelin thrower)". Book (PDF 15 / p. 6): "the drills that they believed were most efficient". The authors report the athletes' belief, not an efficiency finding. (2) Baseline item "in-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity ... to avoid training monotony" is tagged **Inferred (transcript)** in the baseline; the entry omits the tag. (3) Missing author point (PDF 14-15 / pp. 5-6): "In beginning athletes, relatively small training loads may lead to large performance improvements, while in athletes with multiyear experience even heavy training routines may result in no performance changes." Checked clean: definition and "general law of biology", "principle of diminishing returns" (PDF 14 / p. 5; fig 1.2); bank metaphor (PDF 15 / p. 6); quantitative vs qualitative modification; three Olympic Games, 3-kg shot, "only during an Olympic season, or one time in a 4-year period"; variable vs stable conflict (all PDF 15 / p. 6). | (1) "using drills they believed were most efficient (for instance, overhead throwing of a 3-kg shot by a javelin thrower)". (2) "**Eric's baseline** (Inferred, course transcript):". (3) Add the beginner vs multiyear sentence to What it is with "(printed pp. 5-6)". |
| `framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations.md` | FIX | (1) **Wrong pointer.** Why it works: "the Hill-curve mechanism this book's own hyperbolic-equation section separately covers, [[framework--explosive-strength-deficit-and-rate-of-force-development-indices]]". The ESD entry does not cover Hill's equation; no entry in this batch does. Hill's equation is on PDF 39 / p. 30. (2) **Voice mislabel.** "**Eric's baseline:** this terminology (Fmm specifically) is the same one the department's velocity-based 1RM estimation protocol implicitly works within". The baseline says nothing about Fmm; this is the writer's reasoning. The VBT item is also tagged in the baseline "Inferred (author uncertain, legacy protocol, see Tensions)". (3) Minor: fig 2.1 unloaded mean reads about 12.6 rad/s, not "roughly 13". Checked clean: 7,257 g and 4,000 g shots, parameter definition, negative parametric relation (PDF 27 / p. 18); fig 2.1: 100 young males, arm extended, 0-8.0 kg, Zatsiorsky, Smirnov & Kulik 1969 (PDF 28 / p. 19); five-activity table and "all relations are negative (inverse)" (PDF 28 / p. 19); Pmm/Vmm/Fmm, Vmm needs minimal resistance and short time, Fmm sufficiently high resistance (PDF 27 / p. 18); cycling gear-ratio example (PDF 28 / p. 19). | (1) Replace with "Hill's equation (F + a)(V + b) = (Fmm + a)b = C appears at printed p. 30 and is not atomized in this batch; see the Supertraining force-velocity entry for the Hill-curve treatment." (2) Relabel as "Inference:" and add "(the VBT protocol itself is a legacy, author-uncertain document per `method-baseline.md` Tension 4)". (3) "about 12.5 rad/s unloaded to under 4 rad/s at 8 kg". |
| `claim--strength-speed-correlation-depends-on-external-resistance.md` | FIX | (1) **Wrong locators.** "(PDF pp. 38-39, 49-50, printed pp. 20, 32.)" Printed 20 = PDF 29, printed 32 = PDF 41. PDF 38-39 and 49-50 hold other content. (2) **Overclaimed novelty and dedup miss.** The entry and `_book.md` present "a scoped, resistance-dependent version of the 'no strength-speed correlation' claim" as the new angle. The vault already carries resistance-dependent strength-speed correlation: Supertraining `claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction` (Fmax:So correlation 0.822 at 80% So down to 0.316 at 20%) and `framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force` ("the strength-speed correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases"). Neither is linked. (3) **Missed author statement that settles the Wisloff point.** Entry: "Inference: this does not resolve whether Wisloff's squat-sprint correlation genuinely contradicts Zatsiorsky's claim". The authors themselves say (PDF 30 / p. 21, sidebar "Why Is Strength Training Vital for Sprinters and Jumpers?"): "Body weight (during the upward takeoff motion) and body mass (during both the horizontal and vertical push-offs) provide high resistance." And PDF 40 / p. 31: no Fmm-Vmm correlation "is true for extreme areas of the force-velocity curve, while intermediate values depend on the Fmm". (4) **Unsupported extension.** "the text notes beginners show a stronger Fmm-Vm relationship than elite/qualified athletes, whose outcomes are more specific and less predictable from Fmm alone (printed p. 20)". Page 20 says only "This is especially true for beginning athletes." (5) "n=100 shoulder flexions": caption says 100 subjects. Checked clean: R² = 0.522 at 6 kg (fig 2.2, PDF 29 / p. 20); R² = 0.692 at 8 kg and R² = 0.015 no load, "no significant correlation" (fig 2.12, PDF 41 / p. 32); "The correlation between maximum maximorum values of Fmm and Vmm is 0: Stronger athletes are not necessarily the fastest ones"; standing vertical jump and table tennis (PDF 29 / p. 20); swim-coach sidebar (PDF 30 / p. 21). | (1) "(PDF pp. 29-30, 40-41; printed pp. 20-21, 31-32.)" (2) Add Related links to both Supertraining entries; rewrite the novelty claim as "primary-source statement of the Fmm-Vmm scoping and the fig 2.2 / 2.12 R² data; the resistance-dependence itself is already in Supertraining's Table 3.1 entry". (3) Replace the Inference with the two author quotes and their pages, then keep a shorter Inference that sprint push-offs are high-resistance tasks by the authors' own account, so Wisloff's squat-sprint correlation is consistent with, not against, this book. Also add the shot-put 50% vs javelin 15-25% weight-room time sidebar (PDF 40 / p. 31) as the authors' own applied example. (4) Cut the clause after "especially true for beginning athletes" or label it Inference. (5) "100 subjects". |
| `framework--explosive-strength-deficit-and-rate-of-force-development-indices.md` | FIX | (1) **Figure 2.9 misread (athlete swapped).** Entry Example: "Training A's maximal strength would not help A's performance if A's sport action stays inside the time-deficit zone". Book (PDF 37 / p. 28): "Training of maximal strength cannot help athlete **B** improve performance if the time of motion is in the time-deficit zone." B is the athlete with the higher ceiling and slower rise. (2) **Table mislabelled.** When to apply: "the elite-motion time-to-peak-force table"; When NOT to apply: "The time-to-peak-force table (0.08-0.21 s across events)". Book (PDF 36 / p. 27): "the time typically required by elite athletes to perform several motions". These are motion durations, compared against Tm; they are not times to peak force. (3) **Dedup miss.** Vault Supertraining `claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction`, `heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice` and `framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force` (starting- and acceleration-strength gradients) cover the same construct family; only the RFD-limiter entry is linked. (4) ODSF baseline mention lacks the "Hawkin Dynamics, adopted practice" tag. Why not NO-GO: the swap is in the Example; the ESD formula, the four indices, the elite motion times and the core quote are all correct. Checked clean: Tm 0.3-0.4 s, final rise under 2-3% disregarded (PDF 35 / p. 26); motion times 0.08-0.10, 0.11-0.12, 0.17-0.18, 0.16-0.18, 0.15-0.18, 0.18-0.21 s (PDF 36 / p. 27); ESD (%) = 100(Fmm − Fm)/Fmm; ESD about 50%; 21.0 m throws, 50-60 kg, 220-240 kg bench, 110-120 kg per arm (PDF 36 / p. 27); IES = Fm/Tm, RC = Fm/(TmW), S-gradient = F0.5/T0.5, A-gradient = F0.5/(Tmax − T0.5); "Fm and the rate of force development, particularly the S-gradient, are not correlated. Strong people do not necessarily possess a high rate of force development." (PDF 37 / p. 28). ESD and S-gradient also exist in the 1e (1e PDF pp. 42, 54). | (1) Example: "Athlete A produces higher force when time is short (time-deficit zone); B is stronger when time is not limited. Training B's maximal strength cannot help B if the sport action stays in the time-deficit zone (printed p. 28, fig 2.9)." (2) Replace both mentions with "elite motion-duration table (time to perform the takeoff or delivery, printed p. 27)", and in _book.md. (3) Add the three Supertraining links; note ESD corresponds to Supertraining's "strength deficit" and S-gradient to its starting-strength gradient (Inference). (4) Add the tag. Also consider adding the authors' "two ways to increase force output: increase Fmm or decrease ESD" with the 50 to 150 kg vs 200 to 300 kg bench example (PDF 36-37 / pp. 27-28). |
| `claim--eccentric-force-exceeds-concentric-and-isometric-force.md` | FIX | (1) **Locator.** "(PDF pp. 43-44, printed pp. 34-35.)" The 50-100% and "up to twice" quotes are printed p. 33 (PDF 42), as the body itself says. (2) **Inference misreads the author's point.** When to apply: "the grip-strength example is a useful coaching illustration that an athlete's ability to sustain a lift does not require the grip muscles to be working maximally in the sense a dynamometer test would show". Book (PDF 43 / p. 34): the example sits in "Eccentric Muscular Action"; maximal grip strength "is only half as high as the force applied to the barbell", yet the grip holds. The point is that the grip, while being forcibly opened, sustains about twice its isometric maximum, i.e. the eccentric/yielding capacity. Checked clean: 50-100%, "up to twice the zero velocity (isometric) force" (PDF 42 / p. 33); fig 2.14 behaviour, "mainly true for qualified athletes and in multijoint motions such as the leg extension", untrained "recently published data" (PDF 43 / p. 34); fewer fibres and lower EMG; grip under 1,000 N, 250 kg, "well over 4,000 N", 2,000 N per arm; downhill running, damaged fibres, "normal precursor", conditioning reduces injury (PDF 43 / p. 34). | (1) "(PDF pp. 42-43, printed pp. 33-34.)" (2) Rewrite as "Inference: the authors use the grip to show yielding force exceeding isometric maximum: grip dynamometer under 1,000 N, yet about 2,000 N per arm is held without the grip opening (printed p. 34)." |
| `framework--stretch-shortening-cycle-mechanisms-and-tendon-elastic-storage.md` | FIX | (1) **Mechanism numbering.** Book (PDF 44 / p. 35): "Second, since the force begins to rise in the eccentric phase, the time available for force development is greater. Countermovement jumps (not drop jumps) are evidence of such an occurrence." The entry's What it is gets this right, but the Example says "countermovement jumps are evidence of the first mechanism", and Related says the jump comparison is what "this entry's mechanism (1) underlies". (2) Example's closing clause "consistent with force-plate practice that runs both variants separately" is the writer's application, unlabelled, and links to a vault entry (`framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate`) that is rated `contested`; say so. (3) Locator "(PDF pp. 44-46, printed pp. 34-36, 38)" should include PDF 43 (printed 34, "Reversible Muscular Action" opener) and PDF 46-47 (printed 37-38, neural mechanisms and fig 2.18). Checked clean: force and power up, energy down (PDF 43 / p. 34); four reasons, Fmm rather than Fm at transition (PDF 44 / p. 35); elastic energy proportional to force and deformation, fig 2.16 stiffer stores less (PDF 44-45 / pp. 35-36); tendon stiffness constant, muscle stiffness rises with tension, elite muscle stiffness exceeds tendon, energy "stored primarily in tendons", horses "short, strong muscles and lengthy, compliant tendons" (PDF 44 / p. 35; fig 2.17 PDF 45 / p. 36); myotatic and Golgi reflexes (PDF 46 / p. 37); fig 2.18 three components, Houk 1974 via Komi 1986 (PDF 47 / p. 38). | (1) Change both to "the second mechanism (longer time for force development)". (2) Prefix the force-plate clause "Inference:" and note the linked Supertraining entry is `contested`. (3) "(PDF pp. 43-47, printed pp. 34-38.)" Optional: add the sidebar point "The objective of drop-jumping drills is ... to accommodate the athletes to fast muscle stretching rather than to immediately generate large forces" (PDF 46 / p. 37). |
| `claim--reversible-muscular-action-is-a-trainable-skill-not-automatic.md` | GO | Non-blocking: end locator "(PDF pp. 47-48, printed pp. 38-39.)" omits PDF 44 / p. 35, which the body already cites correctly for the innate/learned passage. | checked: "a spring in the leg", "even some elite athletes fail to perform this reversible muscular action correctly" (PDF 44 / p. 35); before 1960 accidental, "erroneously called plyometrics", reversible not eccentric is the objective (PDF 47 / p. 38); Golgi inhibition, "even world-class weightlifters cannot compete with triple jumpers in drop jumping", dropping height can then be increased (PDF 47 / p. 38); beginners improve through heavy weightlifting, qualified "this skill is very specific" (PDF 47-48 / pp. 38-39); "Maximal muscular strength (Fmm) and forces produced in fast reversible muscular action (Fm) are not correlated in good athletes and should be treated, and trained, as separate motor abilities" (PDF 48 / p. 39); fig 2.19: 24 weeks, experienced athletes, heavy resistance 70-100% Fm n = 11, explosive n = 10, Häkkinen & Komi 1985 (PDF 48 / p. 39). Mechanism correctly attributed to the authors; baseline item and label match `method-baseline.md` line 85. Optionally add the locator fix during the other fixes. |
| `framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm.md` | FIX | (1) **Wrong attribution of the moment-arm data.** When NOT to apply: "the specific curve shapes and percentages (elbow flexion peak ~90°, shoulder flexion peak near −30°, the 11.5/45.5 mm biceps figures) are single-study data (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1973 and 1992) from a specific population (n=24)". Only fig 2.22 is Zatsiorsky & Raitsin 1973, n = 24 (PDF 50 / p. 41). The 11.5/45.5 mm example carries no citation on the page (PDF 51-52 / pp. 42-43), and there is no Zatsiorsky & Raitsin 1992 in this range. (2) **Voice mislabel.** "**Eric's baseline:** this complements, rather than duplicates, [[supertraining...torque-optimization...]]" is dedup reasoning, not Eric. (3) **Example misuses the source.** The pull-up supination example is given by the authors for secondary moments (PDF 53 / p. 44), not for strength curves or moment-arm geometry, and it duplicates the heuristic entry's example. (4) Locator "(PDF pp. 49-54, printed pp. 40-44)" should be PDF 49-53. Checked clean: strength curve definition, Fmm slightly above knee height (fig 2.20, PDF 48-49 / pp. 39-40); three forms (fig 2.21, Hay & Komi 1992, PDF 49 / p. 40); elbow flexion peak at 90°, about 46% at 0° and 50% at 150°; shoulder 100% at −30°, about 37% at 150° (fig 2.22, PDF 50 / p. 41); sticking point (PDF 50 / p. 41); two transformations; actin-myosin overlap and parallel elastic components; rectus femoris "in some bicyclists"; gastrocnemius and soleus (PDF 51 / p. 42); M = Fd; 11.5 mm at 180°, 45.5 mm at 90°, fourfold (PDF 51-52 / pp. 42-43); fig 2.24 product (PDF 52 / p. 43). | (1) "Fig 2.22 is Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1973), average of 24 athletes; the 11.5/45.5 mm biceps moment-arm figures are given without a source on printed pp. 42-43." (2) Relabel "Inference:" (or move to Related as a dedup note). (3) Replace with an authors' strength-curve example: fig 2.20 (maximal isometric force on the bar peaks when the bar is slightly above knee height, printed pp. 39-40), or the chin-up sidebar ("pronation of the forearm decreases the strength of the elbow curl ... it is simpler to perform chin-ups ... using an underhand grasp", PDF 52 / p. 43). (4) "(PDF pp. 48-53, printed pp. 39-44.)" |
| `framework--types-of-mechanical-resistance-and-training-specificity.md` | FIX | (1) **Incomplete list.** Title and body say "Five Types"; the book also names **compound resistance** (PDF 34-35 / pp. 25-26: rubber band fixed to floor and barbell, so the lifter overcomes weight, inertia and elastic force together). (2) **Locators.** "(PDF pp. 30-31, 33-34, 51-52, printed pp. 21, 23-24, 42-43.)" Types and mechanical feedback are printed 23-26 (PDF 32-35); printed 21 and 42-43 hold no resistance-type content. (3) Minor: mechanical-feedback paragraph (PDF 32 / p. 23) prints the hydrodynamic law as "F = kV²"; the types paragraph (PDF 34 / p. 25) prints "F = k₂V²". Fine to use k₂, but note the book's own inconsistency. 14	# Calculating a Transfer-of-Training Coefficient from Effect Size
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors give a stepwise method to quantify how much an exercise's
17	gains carry over to a different, untrained task. Because performances in different
18	exercises have different modalities (force, time, distance) and are not directly comparable,
19	they use a dimensionless unit, **result gain**, expressed in standard deviations: result
20	gain = gain of performance / standard deviation of performance (printed p. 8). For a group,
21	[(posttraining mean − pretraining mean) / pretraining standard deviation] is "known as the
22	**effect size**" (printed p. 9). The **transfer coefficient** is then: transfer = result gain
23	in the nontrained exercise / result gain in the trained exercise. "The higher the ratio, the
24	greater the transfer of training results" (printed p. 9). The method is demonstrated with a
25	real dataset (Zatsiorsky and Raitsin, 1974): two groups trained isometric knee extension at
26	a fixed joint angle (Group 1: 70°; Group 2: 130°), then both were tested on force at that
27	angle and on barbell squat performance (printed pp. 7-8, figure 1.3). Group 1: force gain
28	410 ± 170 N (result gain 410/340 = 1.2), squat gain 11.5 ± 5.4 kg (result gain 11.5/23 =
29	0.5), transfer = 0.5/1.2 = **0.42**. Group 2: force gain 560 ± 230 N (result gain 560/618 =
30	0.91), squat gain 7.5 ± 4.7 kg (result gain 7.5/28 = 0.27), transfer = 0.27/0.91 = **0.30**.
31	The "Note the results" table (printed p. 9) shows the contrast: Group 2 had the larger
32	absolute force gain in the trained exercise (560 vs. 410 N), while Group 1 had the larger
33	trained-exercise result gain (1.2 vs. 0.91 SD), the higher transfer (0.42 vs. 0.30) and the
34	larger squat gain (11.5 ± 5.4 vs. 7.5 ± 4.7 kg). The authors' conclusion: "Because of the
35	higher transfer of training results, the method used to train the first group better
36	improved the squatting performance" (printed p. 9). (PDF pp. 15-18, printed pp. 6-9; data
37	from Zatsiorsky, V.M. and Raitsin, L.M., 1974, "Transfer of cumulative training effects in
38	strength exercises," Theory and Practice of Physical Culture 6: 7-14.)
39	
40	**Why it works** — The authors give the reason: performances in different exercises have
41	different modalities and are not directly comparable, so a dimensionless unit is needed
42	(printed p. 8). Expressing both the trained and untrained gains in standard deviations before
43	taking their ratio is what lets the coefficient compare methods across different exercises.
44	
45	**When to apply** — As a field-usable method for comparing two training methods' carryover
46	to a target lift or skill, when pre/post data with means and SDs exist for both the trained
47	exercise and the target task: compute each result gain (post minus pre, over the
48	pretraining SD), then divide the nontrained-exercise result gain by the trained-exercise
49	result gain. **Eric's baseline** (adopted practice, Hawkin Dynamics framework, not Eric's
50	own): force-plate reporting follows the Output/Driver/Strategy framework rather than raw
51	values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
52	`hd-odsf-metrics.md`). Inference: the transfer coefficient answers a question ODSF does not
53	address, "did this training method transfer," and would sit beside it rather than inside it.
54	
55	**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own limits (printed p. 9): "Specificity of adaptation
56	increases with the level of sport mastership. The higher an athlete's level of fitness, the
57	more specific the adaptation. The transfer of training gain is lower in good athletes; for
58	beginners, almost all exercises are useful," and elite athletes "should use more specific
59	exercises." In the figure 1.3 experiment "the training effects were more specific for the
60	group that performed exercise at the 130° knee-joint angle." Inference: a coefficient
61	measured in one population does not carry to a population of a different training level. The study is
62	Soviet-era, single-lab evidence; confidence stays `supported`. Inference: do not treat 0.42
63	or 0.30 as universal transfer benchmarks; they belong to this exercise pair, this
64	joint-angle manipulation and this population. The method needs a defined trained exercise
65	and a defined target measured before and after, and cannot be computed retroactively
66	without the pretraining SDs.
67	
68	**Example** — The authors' own conceptual example (printed p. 6): young athletes trained
69	with barbell squats (exercise A) gain, say, 20 kg. Their performance in the standing
70	vertical jump, sprint dash and freestyle swimming (exercises B, C, D) will improve to
71	different degrees: "substantial in the standing jump, relatively small in sprint running, and
72	next to nothing in swimming." No coefficients are computed for this triad in the text.
73

75	[[principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]],

78	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (a
79	qualitative ten-dimension taxonomy of the same specificity problem this quantitative method
80	measures).

14	# Accommodation: Why a Fixed Exercise and Load Stop Producing Gains
15	
16	**What it is** — If an athlete uses the same exercise at the same training load over a
17	long period, performance improvement decreases; the authors call this **accommodation**,
18	"a manifestation... often considered a general law of biology": the response of a
19	biological object to a constant stimulus decreases over time. In training, the stimulus is
20	physical exercise and the response is performance improvement; with increasing training
21	volume or duration the magnitude of adaptation diminishes, which the authors name the
22	**principle of diminishing returns** (printed p. 5). "In beginning athletes, relatively
23	small training loads may lead to large performance improvements, while in athletes with
24	multiyear experience even heavy training routines may result in no performance changes"
25	(printed pp. 5-6). Their own illustration: "A Bizarre
26	Bank Metaphor": imagine a bank that pays a smaller interest rate the longer money stays
27	deposited and the larger the deposit, the opposite of ordinary banking; "this is exactly
28	how our body works," and a real bank with that policy would go out of business (printed p.
29	6, the authors' own analogy). Programs are modified two ways to avoid accommodation:
30	quantitatively (changing training loads, e.g. total weight lifted) or qualitatively
31	(replacing exercises); the text credits elite track and field athletes who avoided
32	accommodation across three consecutive Olympic Games by varying drills year to year: some
33	used the drills they believed were most efficient (for instance, overhead throwing of a 3-kg
34	shot by a javelin thrower) only during an Olympic season, or one time in a 4-year period
35	(printed p. 6). Training programs
36	face a stated conflict: they must be **variable**, to avoid accommodation, while also
37	being **stable/specific**, to satisfy the demand for transfer, since the highest transfer
38	of training occurs with sport-specific exercises (printed p. 6; see
39	[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]]). (PDF pp. 14-15, printed pp.
40	5-6.)
41	
42	**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism only at the level of "a general law of
43	biology" (a constant stimulus produces a decreasing biological response over time); they
44	do not name a specific physiological pathway (e.g. receptor down-regulation, neural
45	habituation) for why training accommodation specifically occurs. Inference: this is
46	consistent with the same diminishing-marginal-adaptation logic that shows up elsewhere in
47	exercise science under different names (e.g. detraining thresholds, novelty effects in
48	motor learning), but the authors do not draw that connection themselves.
49	
50	**When to apply** — As the stated rationale for periodized variation: rotate exercises or
51	load qualitatively/quantitatively once gains from a given routine plateau, rather than
52	running the same protocol indefinitely. **Eric's baseline** (Inferred, course transcript,
53	a course-team position): in-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even
54	when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training
55	monotony for the athlete (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
56	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`).
57	Inference: this is the same accommodation logic Zatsiorsky and Kraemer describe, applied
58	in-season; the baseline material does not itself use the term
59	"accommodation."
60	
61	**When NOT to apply** — The Olympic-cycle example (varying a drill's frequency across a
62	4-year cycle) is a coaching anecdote, not a controlled comparison; the authors do not
63	report data isolating accommodation from other seasonal factors (competition taper,
64	maturation, other training changes) in that example. Inference: the variable-vs-specific
65	tension the authors name is a real constraint, not a rule that resolves in one direction;
66	do not use "avoid accommodation" alone to justify replacing sport-specific exercises with
67	novel ones at the expense of transfer.
68	
69	**Example** — The authors' own worked example: identical triplets with equal starting
70	strength trained with the same 50-kg barbell to failure; once adapted and able to lift 60
71	kg, further gains stopped on the unchanged routine (accommodation) until the load or
72	exercise was changed (see [[framework--four-features-of-the-adaptation-process]] for the
73	full triplet example with all three athletes' outcomes).

for instance, shot mass (the men's shot is 7,257 g, the women's 4,000 g). The **parametric
relation** describes how the dependent variables (Pm, Vm, Fm) change as that parameter is
systematically varied; between Vm and Fm it is typically **negative**: the greater the
force applied to the object, the lower its velocity (printed p. 18). Figure 2.1 (printed p.
19): 100 young males performed fast shoulder flexions with the arm extended while holding a
barbell, load 0 (unloaded arm) to 8.0 kg; mean maximal velocity fell from about 12.6 rad/s
unloaded to under 4 rad/s at 8 kg (read from the figure; data Zatsiorsky, Smirnov & Kulik,
1969). The same negative (inverse) pattern holds across activities with different
parameters: cycling (gear ratio vs. pedaling frequency), rowing, kayaking and canoeing (blade
area vs. blade velocity), uphill/downhill ambulation (slope vs. ambulation speed), throwing

with a waist belt or deduced with a suspension system vs. takeoff velocity); "all relations
are negative (inverse)" (printed p. 19, table). The **maximum maximorum** performance (Pmm,
Vmm, Fmm) is the highest among the maximal values: Vmm requires minimal external resistance
and short movement time (e.g. throwing light objects, the sprint dash); Fmm requires
sufficiently high resistance (printed p. 18). (PDF pp. 27-28, printed pp. 18-19.)

physiological mechanism; it fixes which variable is held constant (the task parameter) and
which is measured, so that a value at one parameter setting (Pm) can be told apart from the
best-of-all-settings value (Pmm). Hill's equation (F + a)(V + b) = (Fmm + a)b = C, which the

14	# Whether Maximal Strength Correlates With Maximal Velocity Depends on the External Resistance
15	
16	**What it is** — The **nonparametric relation** compares Pmm (Vmm, Fmm) with Pm (Vm, Fm, Tm)
17	across athletes, for example bench press Fmm against shot-put distance, or leg-extension Fmm
18	against standing vertical jump height (printed p. 20). Unlike parametric relations (see
19	[[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]]), nonparametric
20	relations "are typically positive": the stronger the athlete, the faster a given movement.
21	"This conclusion is only valid if the resistance overcome by the athlete ... is sufficiently
22	large" (printed p. 20). In tasks where athletes propel their own body, such as standing
23	vertical jumps, "a positive correlation between the Fmm and Vm is commonly observed: Stronger
24	athletes jump higher. This is especially true for beginning athletes." If the resistance is
25	low, the correlation is small; in table tennis strokes "stronger athletes do not have an
26	advantage." "The correlation between maximum maximorum values of Fmm and Vmm is 0: Stronger
27	athletes are not necessarily the fastest ones" (printed p. 20). The data, from shoulder
28	flexion with the arm extended in 100 subjects: with a 6-kg dumbbell, Fmm vs. angular
29	velocity R² = 0.522 (figure 2.2, printed p. 20); with 8 kg, R² = 0.692, "a high correlation";
30	with no load, R² = 0.015, "no significant correlation between Fmm and Vmm" (figure 2.12,
31	printed p. 32). The authors restate the scope twice. On printed p. 31: the dependence of
32	force and velocity on Fmm "is greater in movements with relatively high resistance and slow
33	speed," there is no correlation between Fmm and Vmm, and "this is true for extreme areas of
34	the force-velocity curve, while intermediate values depend on the Fmm." In the chapter
35	summary: "The greater the resistance, the higher the coefficient of the correlation"
36	(printed p. 45). And they place sprinting and jumping on the high-resistance side: "Body
37	weight (during the upward takeoff motion) and body mass (during both the horizontal and
38	vertical push-offs) provide high resistance. If you practice a leg extension without any
39	external resistance, the strength training will be of small value, since there is no
40	positive relation between the maximum maximorum force (Fmm) and the maximum maximorum
41	velocity (Vmm) in this case" (printed p. 21, sidebar "Why Is Strength Training Vital for
42	Sprinters and Jumpers?"). (PDF pp. 29-30, 40-41, 54; printed pp. 20-21, 31-32, 45.)
43	
44	**Why it works** — The authors give the pattern with data and the resistance-dependence as
45	their stated rule, but no neuromuscular mechanism. Inference: as external resistance
46	approaches zero the task tests movement speed, a different motor ability in the authors'
47	terms (printed p. 31), so Fmm has less bearing on the result; as resistance rises the task
48	draws more on force capacity.
49	
50	**When to apply** — As the primary-source statement of the Fmm-Vmm scoping. The library
51	carries a secondhand version in
52	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
53	which marks the "no correlation" claim contested by Wisloff et al. (2004), squat 1RM vs. 10 m
54	sprint time. By the authors' own account on printed p. 21, a sprint push-off is a
55	high-resistance task (body mass during horizontal push-offs), so the book predicts a
56	positive strength-speed relation there. Inference: Wisloff's squat-sprint correlation is
57	consistent with this book, not against it; the book's zero correlation is for Fmm vs. Vmm
58	at near-zero resistance, such as an unloaded arm. The authors' own applied case, "Why Do
59	Shot-Putters and Javelin Throwers Pay Different Attention to Heavy Resistance Training?"
60	(printed p. 31): elite shot-putters spend about 50% of their training time on heavy
61	resistance training, world-class javelin throwers only 15 to 25%. The shot is 7.257 kg (men)
62	or 4 kg (women) and released at nearly 14 m/s; the javelin is 0.8 or 0.6 kg and released
63	above 30 m/s. The shot-putters need a high Fmm because of the high nonparametric correlation
64	between Fmm and delivery velocity; the correlation is low in javelin throwing, smaller still
65	for a table tennis stroke, and 0 for Fmm vs. the Vmm of an unloaded arm.
66	
67	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: do not generalize "stronger athletes are not necessarily faster" to
68	all sport tasks; the same chapter shows R² = 0.522 to 0.692 at 6 to 8 kg. The book says the
69	positive Fmm-Vm correlation in jumping is "especially true for beginning athletes" (printed
70	p. 20) and gives no figures for how it changes with qualification in this passage. The
71	correlations are from one population (100 subjects, one shoulder-flexion task, Zatsiorsky's
72	1969 dissertation data). Inference: the R² values are not general constants.
73	
74	**Example** — The authors' own "Example of Nonparametric Relations" sidebar (printed p. 21):
75	a swim coach measures (a) Fmm in a specific stroke movement against high resistance and (b)
76	swimming velocity. If the correlation were low, maximal strength training would not be worth
77	the time, and muscular endurance and flexibility would matter more. She finds the correlation
78	significant: the better swimmers generate larger forces in specific movements.
79	
80	**Related** — [[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]],
81	[[framework--hill-equation-curvature-ratio-and-force-velocity-testing-limits]],
82	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
83	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
84	(already carries resistance-dependent correlation data: Fmax:So correlation 0.822 at 80% of
85	So down to 0.316 at 20%),
86	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (states
87	that the strength-speed correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance
88	increases). What this entry adds beyond those two is the primary-source Fmm-Vmm scoping, the
89	figure 2.2 and 2.12 R² data, and the authors' own statement that sprint and jump push-offs
90	are high-resistance tasks. See also
91	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

14	# Explosive-Strength Deficit and Four Indices for Rate of Force Development
15	
16	**What it is** — Peak force takes time to develop. Time to peak force, Tm, measured
17	isometrically, is on average "approximately 0.3 to 0.4 s," and "typically, the time to peak
18	force is even longer than 0.4 s"; the final rise is very small (under 2 to 3% of Fm) and the
19	force fluctuates, so the last portion of the curve is usually disregarded (printed p. 26,
20	figure 2.7). The authors compare Tm with "the time typically required by elite athletes to
21	perform several motions" (printed p. 27, table): takeoff in sprint running 0.08-0.10 s, long
22	jump 0.11-0.12 s, high jump 0.17-0.18 s; delivery in the javelin 0.16-0.18 s and shot put
23	0.15-0.18 s; hand takeoff in horse vaulting 0.18-0.21 s. These are durations of the takeoff
24	or delivery, not times to peak force. "The time of motion is less than Tm in all examples
25	given," so Fmm cannot be attained during these motions. As resistance decreases and motion
26	time shortens, the difference between Fm (the maximal force reached in a given condition)
27	and Fmm grows; that difference is the **explosive-strength deficit (ESD)**: ESD (%) =
28	100(Fmm − Fm) / Fmm, "the percentage of an athlete's strength potential that was not used in
29	a given attempt" (printed p. 27, figure 2.8). In takeoffs and deliveries in throwing, ESD is
30	about 50%: among the best shot-putters, throwing 21.0 m, the peak force on the shot is 50 to
31	60 kg, while their bench press Fmm is typically 220 to 240 kg, or 110 to 120 kg per arm, so
32	"the athletes can only use about 50% of Fmm" (printed p. 27). Four indices quantify explosive
33	strength and rate of force development (printed p. 28, symbols from figure 2.7): (a) **index
34	of explosive strength**, IES = Fm/Tm; (b) **reactivity coefficient**, RC = Fm/(TmW), W =
35	athlete's weight, "typically highly correlated with jumping performances, especially with
36	body velocity after a takeoff"; (c) **force gradient** or S-gradient ("S for start") =
37	F0.5/T0.5, F0.5 being half of Fm and T0.5 the time to reach it, the rate of force
38	development at the beginning of an effort; (d) **A-gradient** ("A for acceleration") =
39	F0.5/(Tmax − T0.5), the rate in the late stages of explosive efforts. "Fm and the rate of
40	force development, particularly the S-gradient, are not correlated. Strong people do not
41	necessarily possess a high rate of force development" (printed p. 28). (PDF pp. 35-37,
42	printed pp. 26-28.)
43	
44	**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism as time availability: the sport motion
45	ends before force can rise to Fmm, so the force actually used depends on how fast it rises.
46	They give no neuromuscular account of why rate and peak are independent. Inference: peak

# Explosive-Strength Deficit and Four Indices for Rate of Force Development

**What it is** — Peak force takes time to develop. Time to peak force, Tm, measured
isometrically, is on average "approximately 0.3 to 0.4 s," and "typically, the time to peak
force is even longer than 0.4 s"; the final rise is very small (under 2 to 3% of Fm) and the
force fluctuates, so the last portion of the curve is usually disregarded (printed p. 26,
figure 2.7). The authors compare Tm with "the time typically required by elite athletes to
perform several motions" (printed p. 27, table): takeoff in sprint running 0.08-0.10 s, long
jump 0.11-0.12 s, high jump 0.17-0.18 s; delivery in the javelin 0.16-0.18 s and shot put
0.15-0.18 s; hand takeoff in horse vaulting 0.18-0.21 s. These are durations of the takeoff
or delivery, not times to peak force. "The time of motion is less than Tm in all examples
given," so Fmm cannot be attained during these motions. As resistance decreases and motion
time shortens, the difference between Fm (the maximal force reached in a given condition)
and Fmm grows; that difference is the **explosive-strength deficit (ESD)**: ESD (%) =
100(Fmm − Fm) / Fmm, "the percentage of an athlete's strength potential that was not used in
a given attempt" (printed p. 27, figure 2.8). In takeoffs and deliveries in throwing, ESD is
about 50%: among the best shot-putters, throwing 21.0 m, the peak force on the shot is 50 to
60 kg, while their bench press Fmm is typically 220 to 240 kg, or 110 to 120 kg per arm, so
"the athletes can only use about 50% of Fmm" (printed p. 27). Four indices quantify explosive
strength and rate of force development (printed p. 28, symbols from figure 2.7): (a) **index
of explosive strength**, IES = Fm/Tm; (b) **reactivity coefficient**, RC = Fm/(TmW), W =
athlete's weight, "typically highly correlated with jumping performances, especially with
body velocity after a takeoff"; (c) **force gradient** or S-gradient ("S for start") =
F0.5/T0.5, F0.5 being half of Fm and T0.5 the time to reach it, the rate of force
development at the beginning of an effort; (d) **A-gradient** ("A for acceleration") =
F0.5/(Tmax − T0.5), the rate in the late stages of explosive efforts. "Fm and the rate of
force development, particularly the S-gradient, are not correlated. Strong people do not
necessarily possess a high rate of force development" (printed p. 28). (PDF pp. 35-37,
printed pp. 26-28.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism as time availability: the sport motion
ends before force can rise to Fmm, so the force actually used depends on how fast it rises.
They give no neuromuscular account of why rate and peak are independent. Inference: peak
force and early rate of rise plausibly depend on different properties (how much can be
recruited versus how fast), but the book does not say so here.

**When to apply** — As the primary-source statement, with named indices, of why max-strength
testing alone under-informs short-contact sports. It overlaps
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]];
this entry adds the ESD formula, the four indices, and the elite motion-duration table.
Inference: ESD corresponds to Supertraining's "strength deficit"
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]),
and the S-gradient to its starting-strength gradient
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]); the
two books use different symbols and neither maps them. For how to raise explosive force
once the deficit is known, see
[[principle--raise-fmm-or-cut-the-explosive-strength-deficit]]. **Eric's baseline**
(adopted practice, Hawkin Dynamics framework, not Eric's own): force-plate reporting
separates output, driver and strategy metrics and adds "fluffy" metrics such as RFD only
with a defensible rationale (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). Inference: RC and the S-gradient are
formula-defined candidates for that rationale and could be computed from existing force-time
data; neither source states that link.

**When NOT to apply** — The ESD formula and the four indices come from one Soviet-era
tradition and are not independently replicated in this ingest; confidence stays `supported`.
The motion-duration table (0.08 to 0.21 s) is for elite athletes in the named events.
Inference: do not assume the same durations for other sports or levels without separate
measurement. The authors give ESD of about 50% for takeoffs and throwing deliveries
generally, with the shot-putters as their instance (printed p. 27). Inference: treat it as
their estimate for those movements, not a measured constant for other tasks.

**Example** — The authors' own two-athlete contrast (printed p. 28, figure 2.9): athletes A
and B have different force-time histories. If the time of motion is short (the time-deficit
zone), A is stronger than B; if the movement is long enough to develop maximal force, B is
stronger. "Training of maximal strength cannot help athlete B improve performance if the
time of motion is in the time-deficit zone."

28	role of the rate of force development in the achievement of high-level performance" (printed

30	greater the forces in the natural athletic movement, "the greater the contribution of Fmm

35	than the time needed to reach Fmm, extra Fmm cannot be expressed in it, so further gains have
36	to come from how fast force rises. Faster, better performances shorten the motion further,
37	which is why the balance shifts toward rate of force development as qualification rises
38	(printed p. 28).

42	qualification rises): use it as a sequencing rule, build Fmm first, while strength gains still
43	express themselves in the sport motion, then shift emphasis to rate of force development
44	once further Fmm gains stop showing up in performance. The authors' warning: "Many coaches
45	and athletes make a similar mistake. They continue to train maximal muscular strength when

47	transcript + shared slides, a course-team position): off-season strength work prioritizes

14	# Hill's Equation, the a:Fmm Curvature Ratio, and the Limits of Force-Velocity Testing
15	
16	**What it is** — Experiments on single muscles in laboratory conditions give a
17	force-velocity curve that can be described by Hill's equation (after A.V. Hill, 1938):
18	(F + a)(V + b) = (Fmm + a)b = C, where F is force, V the velocity of muscle shortening, Fmm
19	the maximal isometric tension of that muscle, a a constant with dimensions of force, b a
20	constant with dimensions of velocity, and C a constant with dimensions of power (printed p.
21	30, figure 2.11). The curvature of the force-velocity graph is set by the ratio a:Fmm: "The
22	lower the ratio, the greater the curvature." The ratio "varies from 0.10 to 0.60. Athletes
23	in power sports usually have a ratio higher than 0.30, while endurance athletes and
24	beginners have a ratio that is lower" (printed p. 30; figure 2.11 draws a = 0.1 Fmm and
25	a = 0.6 Fmm). Force-velocity relations in human movements are not identical to those of
26	single muscles, because they superpose several muscles with different features;
27	nevertheless, curves registered in natural movements "can be considered hyperbolic. This
28	approximation is not absolutely accurate, but the accuracy is acceptable for the practical
29	problems of sport training" (printed p. 30). Two testing limits follow (printed p. 31). In
30	fast movements, when the time is too short to develop maximal force, the "real" curve is
31	distorted; to remove the influence of time, experimenters use the **quick-release
32	technique**: the subject develops force isometrically with the body segment mechanically
33	locked, then the lock is released and the segment moves against the given resistance, so
34	the initial conditions are set by the magnitude of force, not the rate or time of force
35	development. Force-velocity relations can also be studied with isokinetic devices, but "the
36	velocity range of modern isokinetic equipment is relatively small, preventing the study of
37	very fast movements." The authors draw three consequences for practice (printed pp. 31-33):
38	a high force cannot be exerted in very fast movements (too fast a start in lifting a barbell
39	from the floor may prevent maximal force when the bar is near the knees); intermediate
40	force and velocity values depend on Fmm, while the extreme areas of the curve do not; and
41	maximal power is reached in the intermediate range, at about one third of Vmm and one half
42	of Fmm, with efficiency greatest at about 20% of Vmm (figure 2.13, after Hill 1950). (PDF
43	pp. 36, 39-42; printed pp. 27, 30-33.)
44	
45	**Why it works** — The book gives the equation and the curvature rule but no physiological
46	reason why power athletes have a higher a:Fmm; the equation itself describes single muscles
47	in the laboratory. Inference: a flatter curve (higher a:Fmm) means force falls off less as
48	velocity rises, which fits the power athletes' need to produce force at speed; the book
49	states the athlete ranges without this reasoning.
50	
51	**When to apply** — When reading a force-velocity profile, the a:Fmm ratio is a single number
52	for curve shape, separate from the curve's end points (Fmm and Vmm). The book's ranges (0.10
53	to 0.60; above 0.30 in power sports; lower in endurance athletes and beginners) give a
54	reference frame for where an athlete's curve sits. When choosing a test, the book's own
55	cautions apply: in very fast movements the measured curve reflects time to develop force as
56	well as the force-velocity relation, and isokinetic devices cannot reach very fast
57	velocities. Inference: the quick-release technique, or a loaded condition slow enough to
58	allow full force development, is the book's answer when rate of force development should be
59	kept out of the measurement.
60	
61	**When NOT to apply** — Hill's equation was derived from single muscles in the laboratory,
62	and the authors call its use for whole human movements an approximation that "is not
63	absolutely accurate." The Supertraining entry
64	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
65	records in vivo data (Perrine and Edgerton 1978) where the curve is not hyperbolic near zero
66	velocity. Inference: do not fit a hyperbola through near-isometric points without checking.
67	The a:Fmm ranges are stated without a cited study or sample on printed p. 30 (figure 2.11 is
68	credited to Zatsiorsky's 1969 dissertation). Inference: treat them as the authors' reference
69	values, not norms. The book does not say how to measure a:Fmm in the field.
70	
71	**Example** — The authors' own sidebar "Why Is a Finger Snap Faster and Stronger Than
72	Unobstructed Finger Extension?" (printed p. 27): simple finger extension lasts about 0.1 s,
73	too short to exert maximal force; in a snap the finger is held under tension against the
74	thumb, so force is not time-limited, and when released the accumulated tension shows in the
75	movement. "A similar technique is used by scientists to get rid of the effects of the rate
76	of force development on force manifestation. It is called the quick-release technique."
77	
78	**Related** — [[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]],

80	[[framework--explosive-strength-deficit-and-rate-of-force-development-indices]],

82	(the Hill curve as a training-specificity principle; the curvature ratio and athlete ranges
83	are not there),
84	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]].

22	(2) because force begins rising during the eccentric phase, the time available for force
23	development is longer than in a pure concentric effort: countermovement jumps, not drop
24	jumps, are given as the authors' example of this mechanism; (3) **peripheral** (muscle and
25	tendon elasticity): stretched muscle or tendon stores elastic (strain) energy proportional
26	to the applied force and the induced deformation, which is recoiled during the concentric
27	phase (figure 2.16: stiffer bodies store less energy per unit force, more compliant bodies
28	store more, for the same force); and (4) **central** (neural/reflex): the myotatic
29	(stretch) reflex adds a positive, force-increasing contribution from spindle discharge
30	during stretch, while the Golgi tendon reflex adds a negative (inhibitory) contribution
31	that limits force when tension rises sharply: the net SSC force enhancement is the
32	combination of a muscle-tendon-elasticity component and these two opposing
33	length-feedback/force-feedback neural components (figure 2.18, from Houk 1974 via Komi
34	1986). Tendon stiffness is constant; muscle stiffness varies with the force exerted: the
35	more tension, the stiffer the active muscle. In elite athletes the active muscle's
36	stiffness can exceed the tendon's stiffness, meaning the tendon deforms more than the
37	muscle under load and so stores most of the elastic energy: the authors note fast-running
38	animals such as horses have "short, strong muscles and lengthy, compliant tendons" that
39	"work as springs" (printed p. 35; figure 2.17, printed p. 36). The sidebar "Muscles and
40	Tendons As Springs in Series" adds: "The objective of drop-jumping drills is, in this case, to
41	accommodate the athletes to fast muscle stretching rather than to immediately generate large
42	forces" (printed p. 37). (PDF pp. 43-47, printed pp. 34-38.)
43

45	(force-time history, elastic energy storage, and the myotatic/Golgi neural interplay), so
46	this is the source's own stated mechanism rather than this entry's inference, except where
47	marked.

41	inhibits extensor muscle activity when tension rises sharply during landing, protecting the

43	response so the athlete can sustain higher landing forces without the reflex-driven force
44	drop. This is the authors' own stated mechanism, not this entry's inference.

a force decrease, which is also why dropping height can then be increased. In beginners,
performance in SSC-type exercises can be improved through other exercises such as heavy
weightlifting; in qualified athletes, "this skill is very specific" and drop-jump
performance does not improve from usual strength exercising alone, even with heavy weights

47-48; printed pp. 35, 38-39.)

inhibits extensor muscle activity when tension rises sharply during landing, protecting the

drop. This is the authors' own stated mechanism, not this entry's inference.

other SSC-specific exercises as their own training category, separate from and not

transcript + slides, a course-team position): training time is deliberately weighted

22	50% at 150°; shoulder flexion is strongest with the arm slightly behind the trunk (−30°,
23	100%) and falls to about 37% at 150° (percentages read from the figure). The weakest
24	positions are the **sticking points**: "The heaviest weight that is lifted through a full
25	range of joint motion cannot be greater than the strength at the weakest point" (printed p.
26	41). Fmm results from muscular forces that undergo two transformations: muscle-tendon forces
27	→ joint moments → strength (end-point force) (printed pp. 41-42). Muscle tension depends on
28	muscle length for two reasons: the overlap of actin and myosin filaments (cross-bridge
29	number) and the contribution of elastic forces, especially from parallel elastic
30	components. As a general rule, with a few exceptions (for example, the rectus femoris in
31	some bicyclists), muscles exert smaller tension at smaller lengths and higher forces when
32	stretched (printed p. 42). As a joint nears the limit of its range, passive elastic forces
33	rise: in arm cocking in pitching, external rotation of the shoulder approaches 180°, and the
34	deformed muscles and soft tissues "contribute to the joint torques that reach maximal
35	values" (printed p. 42, figure 2.23, after Fleisig et al. 1995: 64 N·m and 67 N·m, 310 N,
36	with the arm drawn at 165°). For two-joint muscles, Fmm depends on the position of both
37	joints: with the knee maximally flexed and the ankle plantarflexed, the gastrocnemius cannot
38	produce active force, "a leg position [that] can be used for selective training of the
39	soleus muscle" (printed p. 42). Joint moment = muscle tension × muscle moment arm (M = Fd).
40	The moment arm of the biceps brachii (long head) was 11.5 mm at 180° (full extension) and
41	45.5 mm at 90° of elbow flexion; with equal tension, the moment and the external force would
42	change fourfold (printed pp. 42-43). The joint strength curve is the product of the muscle
43	tension-angle curve and the moment arm-angle curve (figure 2.24, printed p. 43). (PDF pp.
44	48-53, printed pp. 39-44.)

47	externally registered force changes because (1) the muscles produce different tension and
48	(2) the muscular forces act through different moment arms (printed p. 43).

76	underhand grasp than an overhand grasp."

14	# Five Types of Mechanical Resistance Plus Compound Resistance, and Why Equipment Choice Can Break Sport-Movement Specificity
15	
16	**What it is** — Resistance training equipment can be classified by the physical law
17	governing the resistance it provides: **elasticity** (F = k₁D; force proportional to
18	displacement/deformation D, coefficient k₁ = stiffness: springs, stretch cords, rubber
19	bands; force is greatest at the end of range, when deformation is largest); **inertia**
20	(Newton's second law, F = ma; force proportional to the mass being accelerated: hard to
21	isolate purely inertial resistance outside lab devices like an inertia wheel, since gravity
22	and friction intrude); **weight** (F = W + ma, W = object weight, a = vertical
23	acceleration); **hydrodynamic resistance** (F = k₂V², proportional to velocity squared:
24	swimming, rowing, kayaking); and **viscosity-based resistance** (F = k₃V, proportional to
25	velocity, k₃ = a coefficient: used in machines substituting for water-sport dryland
26	training). **Compound resistance** combines them: for instance, one end of a rubber band is
27	fixed to the floor and the other to a barbell, so the lifter overcomes the barbell's weight
28	(constant), its inertia (proportional to its acceleration) and the elastic force (which grows
29	the higher the barbell is lifted) (printed pp. 25-26). The book prints the hydrodynamic law
30	as F = kV² in the mechanical-feedback paragraph (printed p. 23) and as F = k₂V² in the list of
31	resistance types (printed p. 25). Exercises are also classified by whether they have
32	**mechanical feedback**: in a paddling stroke, higher muscular force raises oar velocity, which raises water resistance,
33	which in turn demands more muscular force (a closed loop, figure 2.4): most sport
34	movements have this feedback loop. Mechanical feedback is **absent** specifically in
35	isometric exercise and with isokinetic devices (constant velocity regardless of force
36	applied) (printed p. 23). Inference: so those modes do not reproduce the force-resistance
37	interaction of most sport movements. (PDF pp. 32-35, printed pp. 23-26.)
38	
39	**Why it works** — Inference: because different sport movements are naturally resisted by
40	different physical laws (hydrodynamic for swimming, rowing and kayaking; weight for every
41	exercise in which athletes move their own bodies, which the book classes as weight
42	resistance on printed p. 25), an exercise's resistance type
43	determines how closely its force-velocity demand matches the target movement, independent
44	of which muscles it uses: this is the authors' own point in the dryland-training case
45	study below, though the general "resistance type governs specificity" framing is this
46	entry's synthesis of the mechanics they lay out.
47	
48	**When to apply** — As a checklist when selecting resistance training equipment intended to
49	transfer to a specific sport skill: match the resistance-type profile (elastic, inertial,
50	weight-based, hydrodynamic, viscosity-based) to the target movement's actual resistance
51	type, including compound resistance, not just its visible muscle groups or general movement
52	pattern. This complements
53	[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]] (Chapter 1) by giving a
54	mechanical reason, in addition to a measured-transfer-coefficient reason, that an exercise
55	might fail to transfer.
56	
57	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a mechanics-based classification, not itself a
58	ranked hierarchy of "better" and "worse" resistance types; each type is appropriate for
59	different training goals (elastic resistance for end-range loading, isokinetic/isometric
60	for eliminating the confound of a changing external load during rehab-style force testing,
61	despite lacking mechanical feedback). Do not treat "lacks mechanical feedback" as
62	disqualifying isometric or isokinetic training outright; the authors present it as a
63	descriptive difference from most sport movements, not a stated flaw.
64	
65	**Example** — The authors' own case study, "Selection of Dryland Exercises for Swimmers"
66	(printed p. 25): a swim coach trialed extensible rubber bands (elastic resistance, pulling
67	force increased through the pull, unlike the customary stroke), a weightlifting pulley
68	machine (near-constant resistance across the pull, but the athletes could not relax at the
69	end of motion, unlike a real stroke), and friction/hydrodynamic training devices (either
70	constant resistance or resistance proportional to pull velocity, both meant to mimic water
71	resistance): none matched the true stroke's resistance profile (proportional to the
72	squared hand velocity relative to water) exactly, illustrating why matching a device's
73	underlying resistance law to the sport movement's own is harder than it looks, even when
74	targeting the same muscle groups and general movement pattern.
75	
76	**Related** — [[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]],
77	[[claim--strength-speed-correlation-depends-on-external-resistance]].

14	# Near-Full Limb Extension Maximizes End-Point Force in Isometric and Heavy Efforts, but Not in Takeoffs
15	
16	**What it is** — In a single-joint task, strength (the force exerted at the end effector)
17	equals the joint moment divided by the moment arm of the external force: the smaller that
18	moment arm, the larger the external force the same joint moment can generate (printed p.
19	44). In multilink chains the transformation is more complex, but one case is simple: "The
20	highest forces in leg or arm extension can be exerted when the extremity is almost
21	completely extended" (printed p. 44, figures 2.25 and 2.26). In that position the line of
22	force action passes close to the knee or elbow joint, so the moment arm is small; when the
23	limb is completely extended the force acts along the extremity and its moment arm is close
24	to 0, so "people can sustain extremely large forces" (printed pp. 44-45; figure 2.25 after
25	Zatsiorsky 1992). Figure 2.26 (Hugh-Jones 1947): six seated subjects pushed isometrically on
26	a pedal at five thigh angles and varying knee angles; the largest pushes came at knee angles
27	near 160°, close to the limit, and the caption notes "the ninefold difference between the
28	force magnitudes at different body postures" (printed p. 44). The book states the opposite
29	for dynamic takeoffs (printed p. 22, figure 2.3): in isometric tests the correlation of
30	force with leg length is positive and Fmm is reached close to full extension, but "if the
31	leg extension force is registered in a dynamic movement such as a takeoff in jumping, the
32	dependence is exactly the opposite ... maximal force is generated in the deepest squatting
33	position." The authors explain the switch by resistance type: in the isometric case the
34	resistance is an immovable obstacle, in the takeoff it is the weight and inertia of the
35	athlete's body, and the support leg behaves like a spring, "the greater the deformation
36	(i.e., knee bending), the greater the force" (printed pp. 22-23). (PDF pp. 31-32, 53-54;
37	printed pp. 22-23, 44-45.)
38	
39	**Why it works** — The authors state the mechanism: end-point force = joint moment / moment
40	arm of the external force, so bringing the line of force close to the joint lets the same
41	joint moment produce or bear a larger external force (printed pp. 44-45). For takeoffs they
42	give the spring analogy and the change of resistance type, not a moment-arm account.
43	
44	**When to apply** — The near-extension rule applies to isometric or slow, heavy exertion. The
45	authors connect it to everyday observation: "the heaviest weight can be lifted in
46	semisquatting, not deep squatting, movements" (printed p. 22), and figure 2.25's caption
47	explains "why the heaviest loads can be borne when the legs are almost completely extended"
48	(printed p. 44). Inference: when comparing force-plate or strength-test results collected at
49	different joint angles or limb positions, a result at one position is not comparable with a
50	result at another without accounting for this effect; see
51	[[framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]] for the muscle-tension
52	side of the same relation.
53	
54	**When NOT to apply** — The book says the near-extension rule does not hold for jumping
55	takeoffs: maximal force there is generated in the deepest squatting
56	position (printed p. 22, figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 is a schematic with no data or source on the
57	page. Inference: the ninefold figure belongs to Hugh-Jones's apparatus and six subjects, and
58	does not carry to other set-ups. Inference: near
59	lockout positions carry their own joint-loading considerations, which these pages do not
60	address; do not read "near full extension maximizes force" as a technique or safety
61	recommendation.
62	
63	**Example** — The authors' own figure 2.25 (printed p. 44): the closer the leg is to full
64	extension, the smaller the moment arm d₂ of the load about the knee, and the smaller the knee
65	moment T₂ = Fd₂ needed to bear the force F; when the line of force action passes through a
66	joint center, as drawn at the ankle, that joint's moment is 0.

category: [biomechanics, technique, testing]
