# Near-Full Limb Extension Maximizes End-Point Force in Isometric and Heavy Efforts, but Not in Takeoffs

**What it is** — In a single-joint task, strength (the force exerted at the end effector)
equals the joint moment divided by the moment arm of the external force: the smaller that
moment arm, the larger the external force the same joint moment can generate (printed p.
44). In multilink chains the transformation is more complex, but one case is simple: "The
highest forces in leg or arm extension can be exerted when the extremity is almost
completely extended" (printed p. 44, figures 2.25 and 2.26). In that position the line of
force action passes close to the knee or elbow joint, so the moment arm is small; when the
limb is completely extended the force acts along the extremity and its moment arm is close
to 0, so "people can sustain extremely large forces" (printed pp. 44-45; figure 2.25 after
Zatsiorsky 1992). Figure 2.26 (Hugh-Jones 1947): six seated subjects pushed isometrically on
a pedal at five thigh angles and varying knee angles; the largest pushes came at knee angles
near 160°, close to the limit, and the caption notes "the ninefold difference between the
force magnitudes at different body postures" (printed p. 44). The book states the opposite
for dynamic takeoffs (printed p. 22, figure 2.3): in isometric tests the correlation of
force with leg length is positive and Fmm is reached close to full extension, but "if the
leg extension force is registered in a dynamic movement such as a takeoff in jumping, the
dependence is exactly the opposite ... maximal force is generated in the deepest squatting
position." The authors explain the switch by resistance type: in the isometric case the
resistance is an immovable obstacle, in the takeoff it is the weight and inertia of the
athlete's body, and the support leg behaves like a spring, "the greater the deformation
(i.e., knee bending), the greater the force" (printed pp. 22-23). (PDF pp. 31-32, 53-54;
printed pp. 22-23, 44-45.)

**Why it works** — The authors state the mechanism: end-point force = joint moment / moment
arm of the external force, so bringing the line of force close to the joint lets the same
joint moment produce or bear a larger external force (printed pp. 44-45). For takeoffs they
give the spring analogy and the change of resistance type, not a moment-arm account.

**When to apply** — The near-extension rule applies to isometric or slow, heavy exertion. The
authors connect it to everyday observation: "the heaviest weight can be lifted in
semisquatting, not deep squatting, movements" (printed p. 22), and figure 2.25's caption
explains "why the heaviest loads can be borne when the legs are almost completely extended"
(printed p. 44). Inference: when comparing force-plate or strength-test results collected at
different joint angles or limb positions, a result at one position is not comparable with a
result at another without accounting for this effect; see
[[framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]] for the muscle-tension
side of the same relation.

**When NOT to apply** — The book says the near-extension rule does not hold for jumping
takeoffs: maximal force there is generated in the deepest squatting
position (printed p. 22, figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 is a schematic with no data or source on the
page. Inference: the ninefold figure belongs to Hugh-Jones's apparatus and six subjects, and
does not carry to other set-ups. Inference: near
lockout positions carry their own joint-loading considerations, which these pages do not
address; do not read "near full extension maximizes force" as a technique or safety
recommendation.

**Example** — The authors' own figure 2.25 (printed p. 44): the closer the leg is to full
extension, the smaller the moment arm d₂ of the load about the knee, and the smaller the knee
moment T₂ = Fd₂ needed to bear the force F; when the line of force action passes through a
joint center, as drawn at the ankle, that joint's moment is 0.

**Related** — [[framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]] (also
carries the book's pitching-shoulder example, which the authors give for passive elastic
forces near the end of range, not for end-point force),
[[framework--types-of-mechanical-resistance-and-training-specificity]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]].

14	# Athletes Tend to Self-Organize Technique to Minimize Secondary (Non-Primary) Joint Moments
15	
16	**What it is** — Muscles produce moments of force not only in the intended (primary)
17	direction but also in other directions (secondary moments); the body counterbalances
18	unwanted secondary moments by activating additional muscles, which increases the number of
19	active muscles while sometimes decreasing net strength in the primary direction (worked
20	example: a forceful arm supination with the elbow flexed at a right angle, as in driving a
21	screw: the triceps, though not a supinator, becomes active to counterbalance the flexion
22	moment the supinating biceps also produces as a secondary effect; printed p. 43). The
23	chin-up sidebar on the same page shows the same biceps coupling from the other side: with the
24	arm pronated the biceps cannot generate its maximal tension, so pronation decreases elbow
25	curl strength and chin-ups are simpler with an underhand grasp (printed p. 43). For the
26	self-organization point itself the authors give one example: gymnasts performing pull-ups
27	on rings always supinate the arms while flexing the elbows; "nobody teaches them to do so; the movement pattern is simply more convenient
28	for the performers" (printed p. 44). The authors present this as their stated general
29	observation, "athletes tend to perform forceful movements in a way that minimizes
30	secondary moments," with the ring pull-up as its only illustration. (PDF pp. 52-53,
31	printed pp. 43-44.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — Inference: the authors do not name a specific motor-control mechanism
34	(e.g. an optimization process in motor learning, energy-cost minimization, or proprioceptive
35	feedback) for why athletes converge on secondary-moment-minimizing technique without
36	coaching; they state the observation and the biomechanical reason it would be advantageous
37	(fewer competing/counterbalancing muscles active, potentially preserving more net force for
38	the primary moment), but not a mechanism for how an untaught athlete arrives at that
39	pattern.
40	
41	**When to apply** — Inference: as a caution against over-coaching a self-selected technique
42	detail that may already reflect an athlete's own biomechanically favorable adaptation (e.g.
43	a specific grip rotation or limb orientation an athlete adopts without being taught it)
44	before assuming it needs correction; worth checking whether an unprompted technique quirk
45	reduces secondary-moment demand rather than treating it as a fault by default.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single stated observation illustrated with one example
48	(pull-up arm supination); the authors do not provide data (EMG, force measurement across
49	technique variants, or a controlled comparison) showing that self-selected technique
50	actually reduces secondary moments more than an alternative, taught technique would.
51	Confidence is `untested`: treat this as a plausible coaching heuristic worth watching for,
52	not an established finding. Do not use it to dismiss legitimate technique coaching broadly;
53	the claim is narrow (secondary-moment minimization specifically), not a general argument
54	against coaching intervention.
55	
56	**Example** — Inference: a lineman who naturally rotates his hand/wrist into a particular
57	position during a punch or block, without being cued to, may be self-organizing to reduce a
58	secondary moment at the wrist or elbow; before correcting it, a coach could check whether
59	the self-selected position is biomechanically explicable (as the ring-gymnast supination
60	example is) rather than assuming it is simply incorrect technique. This application to a
61	football skill is this entry's own extension, not stated in the source.
62	
63	**Related** — [[framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]].

# Athletes Tend to Self-Organize Technique to Minimize Secondary (Non-Primary) Joint Moments

**What it is** — Muscles produce moments of force not only in the intended (primary)
direction but also in other directions (secondary moments); the body counterbalances
unwanted secondary moments by activating additional muscles, which increases the number of
active muscles while sometimes decreasing net strength in the primary direction (worked
example: a forceful arm supination with the elbow flexed at a right angle, as in driving a
screw: the triceps, though not a supinator, becomes active to counterbalance the flexion
moment the supinating biceps also produces as a secondary effect; printed p. 43). The
chin-up sidebar on the same page shows the same biceps coupling from the other side: with the
arm pronated the biceps cannot generate its maximal tension, so pronation decreases elbow
curl strength and chin-ups are simpler with an underhand grasp (printed p. 43). For the
self-organization point itself the authors give one example: gymnasts performing pull-ups
on rings always supinate the arms while flexing the elbows; "nobody teaches them to do so; the movement pattern is simply more convenient
for the performers" (printed p. 44). The authors present this as their stated general
observation, "athletes tend to perform forceful movements in a way that minimizes
secondary moments," with the ring pull-up as its only illustration. (PDF pp. 52-53,
printed pp. 43-44.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the authors do not name a specific motor-control mechanism
(e.g. an optimization process in motor learning, energy-cost minimization, or proprioceptive
feedback) for why athletes converge on secondary-moment-minimizing technique without
coaching; they state the observation and the biomechanical reason it would be advantageous
(fewer competing/counterbalancing muscles active, potentially preserving more net force for
the primary moment), but not a mechanism for how an untaught athlete arrives at that
pattern.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a caution against over-coaching a self-selected technique
detail that may already reflect an athlete's own biomechanically favorable adaptation (e.g.
a specific grip rotation or limb orientation an athlete adopts without being taught it)
before assuming it needs correction; worth checking whether an unprompted technique quirk
reduces secondary-moment demand rather than treating it as a fault by default.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single stated observation illustrated with one example
(pull-up arm supination); the authors do not provide data (EMG, force measurement across
technique variants, or a controlled comparison) showing that self-selected technique
actually reduces secondary moments more than an alternative, taught technique would.
Confidence is `untested`: treat this as a plausible coaching heuristic worth watching for,
not an established finding. Do not use it to dismiss legitimate technique coaching broadly;
the claim is narrow (secondary-moment minimization specifically), not a general argument
against coaching intervention.

**Example** — Inference: a lineman who naturally rotates his hand/wrist into a particular
position during a punch or block, without being cued to, may be self-organizing to reduce a
secondary moment at the wrist or elbow; before correcting it, a coach could check whether
the self-selected position is biomechanically explicable (as the ring-gymnast supination
example is) rather than assuming it is simply incorrect technique. This application to a
football skill is this entry's own extension, not stated in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]].

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent, falsification brief; did not write the entries or the fixes). Date: 2026-09-27.
Scope: all 17 entries in `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/` (15 round-1 entries plus the new Hill and raise-Fmm-or-cut-ESD entries, reviewed in full against `staging/review_book_prompt.md`) and `_book.md`.
Standards read first: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`, `staging/review_book_prompt.md`, `docs/method-baseline.md`, `staging/review_zatsiorsky_ch1-2_opus.md`, `staging/fixes_zatsiorsky_ch1-2_applied.md`. The fixer log was not trusted; every claim below was checked in the files and on the page images.

## What was opened and what was run

- **Source location.** Neither PDF is under `staging\books\` (that folder holds only the Supertraining PDF). The 2e was read from the Drive path in `_book.md` (`G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\TB's Training Info (snapshot 2026-09-26)\SC Books\S&C Books\Science and Practice of Strength Training- Zatsiorsky.pdf`, 247 pages). The 1e was probed at `G:\My Drive\Athletic Performance & Sports Science\Strength and Conditioning Resources\From Coach Lowe\Science and Practice of Strength Training.pdf` (118 pages).
